claim: The fitted model estimates the maximum efficacy of Paxlovid for reducing the replication rate of SARS-CoV-2 viruses as 0.91.
source: By fitting a mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 kinetics within a single patient to the viral load measurements, we estimate the rates at which viral particles infect susceptible host cells (β), infected cells are cleared (δ), and infected cells release viral particles (π), as well as the maximum efficacy of Paxlovid for reducing the replication rate of SARS-CoV-2 viruses (0.91) (National Library of Medicine (U.S.), 2023; Hammond et al., 2022; Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim cites National Library of Medicine (U.S.), 2023 and Hammond et al., 2022, and references supplementary files with model fitting results.

claim: The fitted model simulates viral load trajectories that mirror the observed data in the treated and untreated cohorts.
source: The fitted model simulates viral load trajectories that mirror the observed data in the treated and untreated cohorts (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim references Figure 1A, B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing model fit to data.

claim: Fast-acting antiviral drugs like Paxlovid have the potential to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission while improving patient outcomes.
source: In conclusion, fast-acting antiviral drugs like Paxlovid have the potential to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission while improving patient outcomes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: The development of global distribution programs that provide rapid and equitable access to Paxlovid could enhance our ability to combat COVID-19.
source: The development of global distribution programs that provide rapid and equitable access could enhance our ability to combat COVID-19 as the virus and the landscape of immunity continue to evolve.
evidence: The claim is stated in the conclusion as a recommendation.

claim: The EHR data includes daily viral titer measurements starting from the fourth day after symptom onset.
source: The EHR data includes age, sex, vaccination history, drug prescriptions, symptoms, and daily viral titer measurements starting from the fourth day after symptom onset (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction describing the data.

claim: Each patient record includes daily viral titer measurements between 8 and 15 days post symptom onset.
source: Each patient record includes demographic information, drug administration data, symptoms, laboratory test results, and daily viral titer measurements (i.e. RT-qPCR cycle threshold (Ct) values) between 8 and 15 days post symptom onset.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data.

claim: Cohorts were matched based on age group, gender, and vaccination status.
source: We matched based on age group (5~17, 18~50, 51~65, >65), gender, and vaccination status (i.e. fully vaccinated or not).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing cohort selection.

claim: The model incorporates a gradual decline in Paxlovid efficacy following a five-day course of treatment.
source: We incorporate a gradual decline in Paxlovid efficacy following a five-day course of treatment, using a pharmacokinetic model introduced in a recent study of Paxlovid rebound dynamics.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the model.

claim: The study used software MONOLIX 2021R1 to calibrate parameters using a nonlinear mixed-effect model.
source: We calibrate parameters in the model using a nonlinear mixed-effect model with both the fixed effect (population scale) and random effect (individual scale) in software MONOLIX 2021R1 (Traynard et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Traynard et al., 2020 as the source for the software.

claim: Fixed effects are population parameters that govern all patients.
source: Fixed effects are population parameters that govern all patients and random effects are variable across individuals.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section defining model terms.

claim: Random effects are variable across individuals.
source: Fixed effects are population parameters that govern all patients and random effects are variable across individuals.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section defining model terms.

claim: The study confirmed the convergence of parameter estimates via trace plots.
source: We used the Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization (SAEM) algorithm to estimate these parameters (Miao et al., 2011; Traynard et al., 2020) assuming fixed values for the initial numbers of infecting virions and susceptible target cells following Ke et al., 2021 and confirmed the convergence of the estimates via trace plots.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing model validation.

claim: The SAEM algorithm is an established method in population pharmacology modeling with clear convergence indicators.
source: The SAEM algorithm is an established method in population pharmacology modeling with clear convergence indicators (Delyon et al., 1999; Population parameter using SAEM algorithm, 2016).
evidence: The claim cites Delyon et al., 1999 and Population parameter using SAEM algorithm, 2016 as sources.

claim: For each simulation, parameter values are randomly selected from triangular distributions with modes and ranges set to the medians and 95% CI estimated from the clinical data.
source: For each simulation, we randomly select parameter values from triangular distributions with modes and ranges set to the medians and 95% CI estimated from the clinical data (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing simulation methodology.

claim: For each treatment initiation time considered, the median and 95% confidence intervals of the reduction in infectiousness are based on 1000 pairs of simulations.
source: For each treatment initiation time considered, we report the median and 95% confidence intervals of the reduction in infectiousness (Δ) based on 1000 pairs of simulations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the analysis approach.
